findings.title: Message loss when queue submission fails after offset is added
findings.body: In SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit, the broad except block catches any exception, including one raised by queue_pool.submit. FixedQueuePool.submit first records the offset as outstanding via add_offset, then attempts work_queue.put. If put raises (e.g., because the queue has been shut down during consumer shutdown), the exception propagates here, and the handler marks the same offset as completed. Since the item was never enqueued or processed, the offset will later be committed by the commit loop, permanently losing that message. This can happen during graceful shutdown or after queue shutdown is initiated while the producer is still submitting.

findings.title: Offsets are completed even when processing raises an exception
findings.body: In OrderedQueueWorker.run, the finally block unconditionally calls offset_tracker.complete_offset after result_processor is invoked. If result_processor raises (e.g., a transient database error not caught internally), the offset is still marked complete and will be committed by the commit loop, causing the message to be skipped without successful processing. The class docstring claims 'Only commits offsets after successful processing', but this implementation commits after any outcome, including failure. While ResultProcessor.__call__ currently swallows exceptions, this strategy may be reused with other result processors that do not, leading to silent data loss.

findings.title: Multiple commit threads share a single OffsetTracker without coordination
findings.body: FixedQueuePool is stored on ResultsStrategyFactory and reused across calls to create_with_partitions, so multiple SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy instances can exist simultaneously (e.g., during rebalancing or assignment changes). Each strategy starts its own commit thread in __init__, and all threads operate on the same queue_pool.offset_tracker. They concurrently call get_committable_offsets and mark_committed. While per-partition locks prevent most corruption, multiple threads may compute the same committable offsets before either marks them committed, leading to duplicate Kafka commits and potential race conditions when one thread updates last_committed while another is still using the old snapshot. This is redundant and can increase commit load; it should be centralized or the tracker should be locked across the entire commit operation.

findings.title: Unbounded queues provide no backpressure
findings.body: FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() with no maxsize, so queues are unbounded. The class docstring claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but there is no fill limit. A slow subscription group can accumulate an unlimited number of work items, leading to unbounded memory growth and potentially crashing the consumer. Consider using a bounded queue with a maximum size and applying backpressure in submit.

findings.title: num_queues can be negative or zero due to unvalidated max_workers
findings.body: In ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ for thread-queue-parallel mode, num_queues=max_workers or 20. If max_workers is a negative integer (e.g., -5), it is truthy, so num_queues becomes -5, resulting in range(-5) producing no queues and no workers. The consumer will accept messages but never process them, and offsets will remain outstanding indefinitely, causing a stall. The CLI option is an arbitrary int with no validation. A positive integer check should be added.

findings.title: get_committable_offsets can be O(n) per commit tick
findings.body: OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets iterates over every integer from last_committed+1 to max_offset for each partition. If there is a large gap (e.g., a stuck message) and many offsets have been accumulated, this range can be very large and the loop executes repeatedly every second in the commit thread. This may cause CPU spikes and delay commits. Consider tracking the next expected offset or using a min-heap of completed offsets to find contiguous runs more efficiently.
